subsystems.name: Antenna
subsystems.role: radiates and receives low-frequency radio waves that can pass through kilometres of ice.

subsystems.name: Transmitter
subsystems.role: generates short, high-power pulses at frequencies of a few megahertz.

subsystems.name: Receiver
subsystems.role: detects the very weak echoes returning from deep interfaces.

subsystems.name: Digital processing unit
subsystems.role: turns raw echoes into radargrams and corrects for ionospheric and surface clutter.

subsystems.name: Timing and navigation
subsystems.role: provides precise clock and orbit knowledge so echoes can be located on the surface.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal
subsystems.role: supplies electricity and keeps electronics within safe temperatures in space.

buildSteps.title: Set the science requirements
buildSteps.detail: Choose the target depth, vertical resolution and ice properties; these fix the radar frequency, bandwidth and pulse length.

buildSteps.title: Design the antenna
buildSteps.detail: Model the radiation pattern and select boom length and element geometry for the chosen frequency band.

buildSteps.title: Build the RF electronics
buildSteps.detail: Assemble the transmitter, receiver and timing circuits, using space-qualified components and shielding against radiation.

buildSteps.title: Write the processing chain
buildSteps.detail: Develop algorithms for pulse compression, synthetic aperture focusing, ionospheric distortion correction and surface-clutter removal.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and test on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Test the full instrument in an anechoic chamber and, where possible, over known ice sheets or in a cold chamber to calibrate penetration.

buildSteps.title: Launch and deploy
buildSteps.detail: After launch, deploy the antenna booms and check that the radar returns clean echoes from the surface.

buildSteps.title: Operate and map
buildSteps.detail: Fly repeated passes, record radargrams, model the ionosphere for each pass and convert echo delays into depth profiles.

prerequisites.why: transmitters and receivers at 1–20 MHz are mature from terrestrial ice-penetrating radar.
antennas tens of metres long have flown on Mars orbiters.
Mars' ionosphere is relatively weak, but Earth's and Jupiter's are more distorting, especially at low frequencies.
the processing needed for real-time clutter removal demands high computing power that must survive space radiation.
the depth measurement depends on knowing the spacecraft position and echo time to within metres and nanoseconds.
raw radar data volumes are large, so onboard compression and selective downlink are needed.

pathway.milestone: Orbital sounders map Mars' polar caps and buried glaciers; airborne radar charts Earth's ice sheets.
pathway.unlocks: proven method for detecting liquid water under ice without landing.

pathway.milestone: Radars on Europa Clipper and JUICE sound the ice shells of Europa and Ganymede.
pathway.unlocks: first direct measurements of the depth and structure of an extraterrestrial ocean.

pathway.milestone: Multi-frequency and higher-power sounders distinguish brine from fresh water and resolve thin internal layers.
pathway.unlocks: better estimates of ocean habitability and ice-shell dynamics.

pathway.milestone: Dedicated radar sounders for Enceladus, Titan and other ocean worlds, possibly with real-time onboard processing.
pathway.unlocks: systematic survey of subsurface oceans across the outer solar system.
